newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Volatile commodities see coffee soar, gold slip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Volatile commodities see coffee soar, gold slip.

text.p: World coffee prices extended this year's explosive rally on Wednesday when New York futures hit $2 per pound for the first time since a 1994 Brazil frost scare.
Retail price rises were announced in Britain and France after earlier rises to the consumer in the US, Germany and the Netherlands.
Tight Latin American supply and low stocks were cited to explain the rise of 50 percent in world futures prices for coffee beans since the end of 1996.
At one point on Wednesday, London futures for robusta coffees leapt more than $100 per tonne, chasing New York prices for the arabica types which went to 27-month highs above $2.00/lb.
The London benchmark May robusta contract raced to a new nine-month high of $1,820 but ended off the peak at $1,700 due to aggressive profit-taking, dealers said.
Dealers said the strength was fuelled by supply worries in arabicas and fund buying which pushed New York to the highest since a severe frost in Brazil damaged crops two years ago.
They also said more gains could be on the cards.

"I think the market is going to gather more steam with the tight supply situation especially with arabicas showing no signs of easing," said a Swiss-based trader. "There's a genuine supply concern well into the second half of this year."
French firm Douwe Egberts and five UK roasters said they were raising retail prices by 16-20 percent.

Broker GNI on Wednesday criticised what it called "the idiotic management fad" in commodity markets of cutting costs by operating a hand-to-mouth buying policy through holding low stocks - blaming this for the price volatility.
The roasting industry recently stepped up buying after low 1997/1998 Brazilian crop forecasts and supply disruptions in Central America rumbled the market.
GNI said one factor was that newspapers had signalled the rises in retail prices, and housewives had rushed to the supermarket shelf.
"You just don't have a plentiful supply of coffee right now," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka in New York.

Recent increases in coffee futures were fuelled by unrest among Brazilian port workers who agreed to begin a 72-hour strike on Wednesday. But a port authority spokeswoman said the strike would only affect wood, orange juice and cotton.

Elsewhere in the commodity sector, tumbling gold prices led other precious metals lower, as a proposal that Switzerland sell gold from its reserves to establish a memorial fund for Holocaust victims added to dwindling confidence in the market's strength.
Gold fell to $352.40 by London's close, compared to $359.55 on Tuesday, and New York was also down.
Silver prices were unchanged but platinum and palladium continued their fall from last week when they rallied on delayed export talks in Russia and threats of a strike by Norilsk workers.
After Tuesday's volatility and early highs, base metals on the London Metal Exchange (LME) took a breather on Wednesday, with most prices drifting lower.

Copper prices were high in early London as the market reacted to news of a flooded ASARCO mine in southern Peru, but later trading was slow. Three months copper ended at $2,375, down $20 from Tuesday.

Aluminium had jumped to a 14-month high on Tuesday on fears that squabbling in Russia over the foreign presence in the domestic industry would affect supply. But it eased on Wednesday when the Kontsern Aluminiy producers' group said exports would remain stable.
Up $50 at $8,150 a tonne, nickel showed some recovery from Tuesday's tumble on news of labour problems at Russia's Arctic Norilsk complex that suggested a long stoppage was unlikely.
Lead fell sharply following a bout of option-related selling which pushed the price down to $686.
Crude oil prices, meanwhile, were firm in choppy morning trading, boosted by U.S. data showing lower petroleum stocks.

Front month April Brent contracts traded around $19.55 a barrel for most of the day, up from $19.15 on Tuesday. But dealers said the bullish sentiment evaporated once New York opened as the statistics were already priced into the market.
